title: Derivative Rules
description: Limit definition, power/product/quotient/chain rules, trig, exponential, log and inverse trig derivatives, implicit and logarithmic differentiation.

cards.title: Write the limit definition of the derivative $f'(x)$.
cards.body:
$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$, if the limit exists

It's the limit of secant slopes, i.e. the slope of the **tangent line**. Equivalent form at a point: $f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$.

Tip: Simplify the difference quotient before letting $h \to 0$.
cards.searchQuery: limit definition of the derivative difference quotient

cards.title: Differentiable at $a$ implies continuous at $a$. Is the converse true?
cards.body:
No.

Counterexample: $f(x) = |x|$ is continuous at $0$ but has a **corner** there: slope $-1$ from the left, $+1$ from the right, so $f'(0)$ does not exist. $f$ can also fail to be differentiable at a vertical tangent ($\sqrt[3]{x}$ at $0$) or at a discontinuity.

Key idea: differentiable is a stronger condition than continuous.
cards.searchQuery: differentiable implies continuous converse false absolute value

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\sqrt{x}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$

Rewrite $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ and use the **power rule** $\frac{d}{dx}[x^n] = nx^{n-1}$ (valid for any real $n$): $\frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2}$. Same trick: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{1}{x}\right] = \frac{d}{dx}\left[x^{-1}\right] = -\frac{1}{x^2}$.

Tip: Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers before differentiating.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of square root x 1/(2 sqrt x)

cards.title: Product rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(x)g(x)] = \,?$
cards.body:
$f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x)$

Differentiate **one factor at a time** and add the results.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[x^2 \sin x] = 2x \sin x + x^2 \cos x$.
Watch out: the derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives, $f'(x)g'(x)$.
cards.searchQuery: product rule derivative formula

cards.title: Quotient rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{f}{g}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}$

The order in the numerator matters because of the **minus sign**; in the product rule it doesn't.

Mnemonic: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below." Check: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{1}{x}\right] = \frac{0 \cdot x - 1 \cdot 1}{x^2} = -\frac{1}{x^2}$.
cards.searchQuery: quotient rule derivative formula

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\tan x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\sec^2 x$

**Quotient rule** on $\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$: $\frac{\cos x \cdot \cos x - \sin x \cdot (-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 x}$, since $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$.

Mnemonic: tan goes to sec squared.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of tan x sec squared

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\sec x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\sec x \tan x$

**Quotient rule** on $\frac{1}{\cos x}$: $\frac{\cos x \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot (-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cos x} \cdot \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$.

Tip: Remember it as sec times tan, with no square.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of sec x sec x tan x

cards.title: Which three of the six trig functions have derivatives that carry a minus sign?
cards.body:
$\cos$, $\cot$ and $\csc$ (the co- functions): $\frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] = -\sin x$, $\frac{d}{dx}[\cot x] = -\csc^2 x$, $\frac{d}{dx}[\csc x] = -\csc x \cot x$

**Pattern**: take the partner's derivative, swap in co-functions, add a minus. $\tan \to \sec^2$ becomes $\cot \to -\csc^2$; $\sec \to \sec \tan$ becomes $\csc \to -\csc \cot$.

Mnemonic: every function whose name starts with 'co' gets a minus sign.
cards.searchQuery: trig derivatives minus sign cos cot csc

cards.title: Chain rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))] = \,?$
cards.body:
$f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$

In words: the derivative of the outside, **evaluated at the inside**, times the derivative of the inside.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[\sin(x^2)] = \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x$.
Watch out: forgetting the inner factor $2x$.
cards.searchQuery: chain rule derivative composite function

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[a^x] = \,?$ (constant $a > 0$)
cards.body:
$a^x \ln a$

Write $a^x = e^{x \ln a}$ and apply the **chain rule**.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[2^x] = 2^x \ln 2$.
Watch out: $x a^{x-1}$ is the power rule, which needs a variable base and a constant exponent.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of a^x ln a exponential base a

cards.title: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ by implicit differentiation: $x^2 + y^2 = 25$.
cards.body:
$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}$

**Differentiate both sides** with respect to $x$: $2x + 2y \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}$. At $(3, 4)$ the tangent slope is $-\frac{3}{4}$.

Watch out: dropping the $\frac{dy}{dx}$ that the chain rule attaches to $y$ terms: $\frac{d}{dx}[y^2] = 2y \frac{dy}{dx}$, not $2y$.
Tip: Collect every $\frac{dy}{dx}$ term on one side, then solve for it last.
cards.searchQuery: implicit differentiation circle x^2+y^2=25 dy/dx

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\arcsin x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$

The formula holds for $-1 < x < 1$. $\sin y = x \implies \cos y \cdot y' = 1 \implies y' = \frac{1}{\cos y} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$, since $\cos y \ge 0$ for $y$ in $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$. $\arccos x$ has the same derivative with a **minus sign**.

Watch out: the slope blows up at $x = \pm 1$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of arcsin x 1/sqrt(1-x^2)

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\arctan x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{1 + x^2}$

The formula holds for all real $x$. $\tan y = x \implies \sec^2 y \cdot y' = 1 \implies y' = \frac{1}{1 + \tan^2 y} = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$. **Read in reverse**: $\int \frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = \arctan x + C$.

Watch out: the denominator is $1 + x^2$ with no square root; that's the arcsin pattern.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of arctan x 1/(1+x^2)

cards.title: $f(x) = x^3 + x$, so $f(1) = 2$. Find $(f^{-1})'(2)$.
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{4}$

$(f^{-1})'(b) = \frac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(b))}$. **Here** $f^{-1}(2) = 1$ and $f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1$, so $f'(1) = 4$.

Watch out: evaluating $f'$ at $2$ instead of at $f^{-1}(2) = 1$ gives $\frac{1}{13}$.
Tip: Find $f^{-1}(b)$ first by solving $f(x) = b$, often by inspection.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of inverse function formula f inverse prime

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\log_a x] = \,?$ ($a > 0$, $a \ne 1$)
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{x \ln a}$

**Change of base**: $\log_a x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln a}$, and $\frac{1}{\ln a}$ is just a constant factor. With $a = e$ this is $\frac{d}{dx}[\ln x] = \frac{1}{x}$.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[\log_{10} x] = \frac{1}{x \ln 10}$.
Watch out: $\ln a$ is a constant, so it stays in the denominator.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of log base a of x 1/(x ln a)

cards.title: Use logarithmic differentiation: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x^x\right] = \,?$ ($x > 0$)
cards.body:
$x^x(\ln x + 1)$

$\ln y = x \ln x \implies \frac{y'}{y} = \ln x + 1 \implies y' = x^x(\ln x + 1)$. Neither the power rule ($x \cdot x^{x-1}$) nor the exponential rule ($x^x \ln x$) applies: **base and exponent both vary**.

Tip: Reach for it when the variable is in both the base and the exponent.
cards.searchQuery: logarithmic differentiation x^x derivative

cards.title: Geometrically, what does $f'(a)$ represent?
cards.body:
The slope of the tangent line to $y = f(x)$ at the point $(a, f(a))$

It's also the **instantaneous rate of change** of $f$ at $x = a$: the limit of average rates of change (secant slopes) over shrinking intervals.

Key idea: the derivative is both a tangent slope and an instantaneous rate of change.
cards.searchQuery: geometric meaning of derivative tangent line slope

cards.title: How does the average rate of change of $f$ on $[a, b]$ differ from the instantaneous rate at $a$?
cards.body:
Average: $\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$, the slope of the secant line. Instantaneous: $f'(a)$, the limit of that quotient as $b \to a$, the slope of the tangent line.

For a position function $s(t)$ these are **average velocity** and (instantaneous) velocity.

Mnemonic: secant for average, tangent for instantaneous.
cards.searchQuery: average rate of change vs instantaneous rate secant tangent

cards.title: For $f(x) = x^2$, the difference quotient $\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$ simplifies to what (for $h \ne 0$)?
cards.body:
$2x + h$

$(x + h)^2 - x^2 = 2xh + h^2$; divide by $h$. Letting $h \to 0$ gives $f'(x) = 2x$. **Simplify before taking the limit**: substituting $h = 0$ first gives the useless $\frac{0}{0}$.

Tip: Expand $(x + h)^2$, cancel the $x^2$ terms, then divide by $h$.
cards.searchQuery: difference quotient f(x+h)-f(x) over h for x squared

cards.title: Equation of the tangent line to $y = x^3$ at $x = 1$?
cards.body:
$y = 3x - 2$

Point: $(1, 1)$. Slope: $y' = 3x^2$, which is $3$ at $x = 1$.

**Point-slope form**: $y - 1 = 3(x - 1)$. A common slip is using the formula $3x^2$ as the slope instead of its value at the point.

Tip: Find the point, then the slope, then use point-slope form.
cards.searchQuery: tangent line to y=x^3 at x=1

cards.title: The tangent line to a curve at a point has slope $m \ne 0$. What is the slope of the normal line there?
cards.body:
$-\frac{1}{m}$

The normal line is **perpendicular** to the tangent, and perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$. If $m = 0$, the normal line is vertical.

Example: tangent slope $3$ gives normal slope $-\frac{1}{3}$.
Mnemonic: flip it and change the sign.
cards.searchQuery: slope of normal line negative reciprocal of tangent slope

cards.title: In Leibniz notation, what does $\left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x = a}$ mean when $y = f(x)$?
cards.body:
$f'(a)$: the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ evaluated at $x = a$

$\frac{dy}{dx}$ isn't really a fraction, but it often acts like one, as in the **chain rule** $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}$.

Tip: The vertical bar means 'evaluate at'.
cards.searchQuery: Leibniz notation dy/dx evaluated at x=a

cards.title: Position $s(t) = t^2 + 3t$ (meters, $t$ in seconds). What is the instantaneous velocity at $t = 2$?
cards.body:
$7\ \mathrm{m/s}$

$v(t) = s'(t) = 2t + 3$, so $v(2) = 7$. Compare the **average velocity** on $[0, 2]$: $\frac{s(2) - s(0)}{2} = \frac{10}{2} = 5\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

Tip: Differentiate first, then plug in $t$.
cards.searchQuery: instantaneous velocity from position function derivative

cards.title: If $s(t)$ is position, what physical quantities are $s'(t)$ and $s''(t)$?
cards.body:
$s'(t) = v(t)$ is velocity and $s''(t) = v'(t) = a(t)$ is acceleration

Speed is $|v(t)|$, which ignores direction. The third derivative $s'''(t)$ is called **jerk**.

Watch out: speed is never negative, while velocity carries a sign.
cards.searchQuery: position velocity acceleration derivatives jerk

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}|x| = \,?$ for $x \ne 0$
cards.body:
$\frac{x}{|x|}$

This is $1$ for $x > 0$ and $-1$ for $x < 0$. At $x = 0$ the one-sided slopes $-1$ and $1$ disagree (a **corner**), so $|x|$ is not differentiable there. Chain rule version: $\frac{d}{dx}|u| = \frac{u}{|u|} \cdot u'$.

Tip: Think of the slopes: $-1$ left of $0$, $+1$ right of $0$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of absolute value x over |x|

cards.title: $f(x) = x^2$ for $x \le 1$ and $f(x) = ax + b$ for $x > 1$. Which $a$ and $b$ make $f$ differentiable at $x = 1$?
cards.body:
$a = 2$, $b = -1$

Continuity: $a + b = 1$. Matching slopes: $a$ must equal the slope of $x^2$ at $1$, which is $2$.

So $b = -1$, and $y = 2x - 1$ is the tangent line to $y = x^2$ at $x = 1$. Differentiability needs **both conditions**.

Tip: Match the values first, then match the slopes.
cards.searchQuery: make piecewise function differentiable match value and slope

cards.title: Power rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x^n\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$nx^{n-1}$

This holds for any real exponent $n$. Bring the exponent down, then **lower it by one**: $\frac{d}{dx}[x^7] = 7x^6$. Special cases: $\frac{d}{dx}[x] = 1$, and the derivative of a constant is $0$.

Watch out: the power rule needs a constant exponent; $x^x$ and $2^x$ need other methods.
cards.searchQuery: power rule derivative x^n

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[4x^5 - 3x^2 + 7x - 9\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$20x^4 - 6x + 7$

Differentiate **term by term** (sum and constant multiple rules): $4 \cdot 5x^4 - 3 \cdot 2x + 7 - 0$. The constant $-9$ disappears because a constant's graph is flat.

Tip: Constants vanish and constant multiples pass through.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of polynomial term by term

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{3}{x^2}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-\frac{6}{x^3}$

Rewrite as $3x^{-2}$; the power rule gives $-6x^{-3}$, with **no quotient rule needed**.

Watch out: the exponent goes down by one, from $-2$ to $-3$, not up to $-1$.
Tip: Rewrite $\frac{c}{x^n}$ as $cx^{-n}$ before differentiating.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of 3/x^2 negative exponent

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\sqrt[3]{x^2}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\frac{2}{3}x^{-1/3} = \frac{2}{3\sqrt[3]{x}}$

Rewrite $\sqrt[3]{x^2} = x^{2/3}$ and apply the power rule: $\frac{2}{3}x^{2/3 - 1}$. At $x = 0$ the derivative is undefined: the graph has a **cusp** there.

Tip: Rewrite roots as fractional powers first.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of cube root of x squared fractional exponent

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^x\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$e^x$

The function is its own derivative. That **singles out** $e$: it's the base whose graph has slope $1$ at $x = 0$, i.e. $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{e^h - 1}{h} = 1$.

Watch out: the power rule doesn't apply, so it is not $xe^{x-1}$.
Mnemonic: $e^x$ is its own derivative, forever.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of e^x equals e^x

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\ln x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{x}$

This holds for $x > 0$. More generally $\frac{d}{dx} \ln|x| = \frac{1}{x}$ for all $x \ne 0$, which is why an **antiderivative** of $\frac{1}{x}$ is $\ln|x|$. Other bases: $\frac{d}{dx} \log_a x = \frac{1}{x \ln a}$.

Tip: For $\ln u$ the derivative is $\frac{u'}{u}$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of ln x equals 1/x

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{\pi}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$0$

$e^\pi \approx 23.14$ is a **constant**: no $x$ appears. Neither the exponential rule (which would give $e^\pi$) nor the power rule applies; the derivative of any constant is $0$.

Watch out: a constant, even one as scary as $e^\pi$, has derivative $0$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of e to the pi constant is zero

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\sin x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\cos x$

This holds when $x$ is in radians. It comes from the **limit definition**, using $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{h} = 1$ and $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\cos h - 1}{h} = 0$. Check on the graph: $\sin x$ is steepest at $x = 0$, where $\cos 0 = 1$, and flat at $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, where $\cos \frac{\pi}{2} = 0$.

Watch out: this rule needs radians.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of sin x equals cos x radians

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\cos x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-\sin x$

The **minus sign** matches the graph: $\cos x$ decreases on $(0, \pi)$, where $\sin x > 0$. Derivative cycle: $\sin \to \cos \to -\sin \to -\cos \to \sin$.

Watch out: the derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$, not $\sin x$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of cos x equals negative sin x

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\cot x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-\csc^2 x$

**Quotient rule** on $\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$: $\frac{-\sin^2 x - \cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x} = -\frac{1}{\sin^2 x}$. It mirrors $\frac{d}{dx}[\tan x] = \sec^2 x$, with co-functions and a minus sign.

Mnemonic: cot is the co-function of tan, so it gets a minus sign.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of cot x negative csc squared

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\csc x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-\csc x \cot x$

**Quotient rule** on $\frac{1}{\sin x}$: $\frac{0 - \cos x}{\sin^2 x} = -\frac{1}{\sin x} \cdot \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$. It mirrors $\frac{d}{dx}[\sec x] = \sec x \tan x$, with co-functions and a minus sign.

Mnemonic: csc is the co-function partner of sec, so it gets a minus sign.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of csc x negative csc x cot x

cards.title: For $f(x) = x^3$, the difference quotient $\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$ simplifies to what (for $h \ne 0$)?
cards.body:
$3x^2 + 3xh + h^2$

Expand $(x + h)^3 = x^3 + 3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3$, subtract $x^3$ and divide by $h$. Letting $h \to 0$ leaves $f'(x) = 3x^2$.

Tip: after dividing by $h$, every leftover term except $3x^2$ still has a factor of $h$.
cards.searchQuery: difference quotient x cubed simplifies 3x^2+3xh+h^2

cards.title: Use the limit definition to find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{1}{x}\right]$.
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{1}{x^2}$

Combine the fractions: $\frac{\frac{1}{x + h} - \frac{1}{x}}{h} = \frac{-h}{x(x + h)\,h} = \frac{-1}{x(x + h)}$. As $h \to 0$ this tends to $-\frac{1}{x^2}$.

Tip: with a fraction in the numerator, **combine over a common denominator** before cancelling $h$.
cards.searchQuery: limit definition derivative of 1/x gives -1/x^2

cards.title: $P(t)$ is the number of bacteria after $t$ hours. What are the units of $P'(t)$?
cards.body:
Bacteria per hour

$P'(t)$ is the limit of $\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta t}$, so its units are **units of output per unit of input**.

Example: $P'(3) = 500$ means the population is growing at about $500$ bacteria per hour at $t = 3$.
cards.searchQuery: units of the derivative bacteria per hour rate of change

cards.title: $C(x)$ is the cost of producing $x$ items. What does $C'(100)$ approximate?
cards.body:
The extra cost of producing the $101$st item.

$C'(x)$ is the **marginal cost**: the rate of change of cost per additional item. It approximates $C(101) - C(100)$ because one item is small next to $100$.

Watch out: marginal cost is not the average cost $\frac{C(x)}{x}$.
cards.searchQuery: marginal cost derivative of cost function meaning

cards.title: $f(x) = |x - 2|$. What is the left-hand derivative $\lim_{h \to 0^-} \dfrac{f(2 + h) - f(2)}{h}$?
cards.body:
$-1$

Here $f(2 + h) - f(2) = |h|$, and for $h < 0$, $|h| = -h$, so the quotient is $\frac{-h}{h} = -1$.

The right-hand derivative is $+1$. Since the **one-sided derivatives differ**, $f'(2)$ does not exist.
cards.searchQuery: left-hand derivative of absolute value at corner

cards.title: In what four ways can $f$ fail to be differentiable at $x = a$?
cards.body:
A **corner**, a **cusp**, a **vertical tangent**, or a **discontinuity** at $a$.

- Corner: different one-sided slopes, like $|x|$ at $0$.
- Cusp: slopes tend to $+\infty$ on one side and $-\infty$ on the other, like $x^{2/3}$ at $0$.
- Vertical tangent: slope tends to $\pm\infty$ on both sides, like $\sqrt[3]{x}$ at $0$.
- Discontinuity: no limit of the quotient at all.

Key idea: a smooth graph has a unique non-vertical tangent at every point.
cards.searchQuery: ways function fails differentiable corner cusp vertical tangent

cards.title: Why does differentiability at $a$ force continuity at $a$?
cards.body:
Because $f(x) - f(a) = \dfrac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} \cdot (x - a)$, and the right side tends to $f'(a) \cdot 0 = 0$.

So $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$, which is exactly continuity at $a$.

Watch out: the converse is false: $|x|$ is continuous at $0$ but has no derivative there.
cards.searchQuery: why differentiable implies continuous proof difference quotient

cards.title: Constant multiple rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[c\,f(x)] = \,?$
cards.body:
$c\,f'(x)$

A constant factor just rides along: **pull it out**, differentiate, and put it back.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[5x^3] = 5 \cdot 3x^2 = 15x^2$.
Watch out: this works only for constants. In $x \sin x$ the factor $x$ varies, so you need the product rule.
cards.searchQuery: constant multiple rule derivative

cards.title: Sum rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(x) + g(x)] = \,?$
cards.body:
$f'(x) + g'(x)$

Differentiate **term by term**; the same holds for differences.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[x^2 + \sin x] = 2x + \cos x$.
Watch out: this term-by-term rule is for sums only; products and quotients need their own rules.
cards.searchQuery: sum rule for derivatives term by term

cards.title: Reciprocal rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{1}{g(x)}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{g'(x)}{g(x)^2}$

It's the quotient rule with $f = 1$ (so $f' = 0$), or the chain rule applied to $g^{-1}$.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{1}{x^2 + 1}\right] = -\frac{2x}{(x^2 + 1)^2}$.
Watch out: the derivative of $\frac{1}{g}$ is not $\frac{1}{g'}$.
cards.searchQuery: reciprocal rule derivative of 1 over g(x)

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\pi^x\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\pi^x \ln \pi$

This is $\frac{d}{dx}[a^x] = a^x \ln a$ with $a = \pi$: the base is a **constant** and the exponent is the variable.

Watch out: don't use the power rule here. That's for $x^\pi$, whose derivative is $\pi x^{\pi - 1}$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of pi to the x power exponential constant base

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x^{\pi}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\pi x^{\pi - 1}$

The exponent $\pi$ is a constant, so the **power rule** applies: bring it down and subtract one.

Watch out: this is not $\pi^x \ln \pi$, which is the derivative of $\pi^x$ (variable exponent).
cards.searchQuery: derivative of x to the pi power rule constant exponent

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[(x^2 + 1)e^x\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$(x + 1)^2 e^x$

Take $f = x^2 + 1$ and $g = e^x$: $2x e^x + (x^2 + 1)e^x = e^x(x^2 + 2x + 1)$.

Tip: **factor out the common factor** at the end; it keeps the answer short and often reveals the zeros.
cards.searchQuery: product rule example (x^2+1)e^x derivative

cards.title: Product rule for three factors: $(fgh)' = \,?$
cards.body:
$f'gh + fg'h + fgh'$

Differentiate **one factor at a time** and leave the other two alone, so each term has exactly one prime.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[x \, e^x \sin x] = e^x \sin x + x e^x \sin x + x e^x \cos x$.
Watch out: forgetting one of the three terms is the usual slip.
cards.searchQuery: product rule for three factors formula (fgh)'

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1 - x^2}{(x^2 + 1)^2}$

Numerator: $1 \cdot (x^2 + 1) - x \cdot 2x = 1 - x^2$. The denominator is the square of the original denominator.

Tip: the sign of the derivative is the sign of $1 - x^2$, so the function increases on $(-1, 1)$.
cards.searchQuery: quotient rule example x over x^2+1 derivative

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[x \ln x] = \,?$ ($x > 0$)
cards.body:
$\ln x + 1$

Product rule: $1 \cdot \ln x + x \cdot \frac{1}{x}$. The extra $+1$ comes from $x \cdot \frac{1}{x}$.

Example: the derivative is $0$ at $x = \frac{1}{e}$, where $x \ln x$ has its minimum value $-\frac{1}{e}$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of x ln x product rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{kx}\right] = \,?$ ($k$ a constant)
cards.body:
$k\,e^{kx}$

Chain rule: the outside is $e^u$, the inside is $u = kx$ with $u' = k$.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[e^{-3x}\right] = -3e^{-3x}$.
Watch out: $e^{kx}$ is its own derivative only when $k = 1$; otherwise **the constant comes out front**.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of e^(kx) chain rule constant k

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{-x^2}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-2x\,e^{-x^2}$

The outside is $e^u$ and the inside is $u = -x^2$ with $u' = -2x$.

Tip: this is the slope of the bell curve. It is positive for $x < 0$, zero at $x = 0$ (the peak) and negative for $x > 0$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of e^(-x^2) bell curve chain rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(x^2 + 1)\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}$

In general $\frac{d}{dx}\ln g(x) = \frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}$: the **derivative of the inside over the inside**.

Watch out: the answer is not $\frac{1}{x^2 + 1}$; that forgets the inner factor $2x$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of ln(x^2+1) chain rule g prime over g

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\ln(\ln x)] = \,?$ ($x > 1$)
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{x \ln x}$

The outer $\ln u$ gives $\frac{1}{u}$ with $u = \ln x$, and $u' = \frac{1}{x}$, so the product is $\frac{1}{\ln x} \cdot \frac{1}{x}$.

Tip: the domain needs $\ln x > 0$, which is why $x > 1$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of ln(ln x) chain rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\sin^2 x\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$2\sin x \cos x$

Read $\sin^2 x$ as $(\sin x)^2$: the outer power gives $2\sin x$, and the inner $\sin x$ gives $\cos x$. By the double-angle identity this equals $\sin 2x$.

Watch out: $\sin^2 x$ is not $\sin(x^2)$; the latter has derivative $2x\cos(x^2)$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of sin squared x chain rule sin 2x

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\cos(x^2)\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-2x \sin(x^2)$

The outside is $\cos u$, which gives $-\sin u$, and the inside is $u = x^2$ with $u' = 2x$.

Watch out: keep the $x^2$ **inside** the sine; don't turn it into $\sin^2 x$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of cos(x^2) chain rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\cos 3x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-3\sin 3x$

The outside gives $-\sin 3x$ and the inside $3x$ contributes the factor $3$.

Watch out: two things are easy to lose, the **minus sign** from $\cos$ and the $3$ from the inside.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of cos 3x chain rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\tan 3x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$3\sec^2 3x$

The outside gives $\sec^2 3x$ and the inside $3x$ contributes a factor of $3$.

Tip: for $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ of $kx$, the derivative gets an extra factor of $k$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of tan 3x sec squared chain rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[(3x^2 + 1)^4\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$24x(3x^2 + 1)^3$

Outer: $u^4 \to 4u^3$. Inner: $3x^2 + 1 \to 6x$. Multiply: $4 \cdot 6x = 24x$.

Key idea: the generalized power rule is $\frac{d}{dx}[g^n] = n\,g^{n-1}\,g'$.
cards.searchQuery: chain rule power example (3x^2+1)^4 derivative

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\sqrt{1 + x^2}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}$

Write it as $(1 + x^2)^{1/2}$: $\frac{1}{2}(1 + x^2)^{-1/2} \cdot 2x$.

Key idea: in general $\frac{d}{dx}\sqrt{g} = \frac{g'}{2\sqrt{g}}$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of sqrt(1+x^2) chain rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\sin\left(e^{x^2}\right)\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$2x\,e^{x^2}\cos\left(e^{x^2}\right)$

There are **three layers**: $\sin u$, then $u = e^v$, then $v = x^2$. Differentiate from the outside in: $\cos(e^{x^2}) \cdot e^{x^2} \cdot 2x$.

Tip: label the layers first; each layer contributes exactly one factor.
cards.searchQuery: chain rule three layers sin(e^(x^2)) derivative

cards.title: Chain rule in Leibniz notation: if $y = f(u)$ and $u = g(x)$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{dy}{du} \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$

The $du$'s seem to cancel, a good memory aid even though $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is not literally a fraction.

Example: $y = u^3$ and $u = 2x + 1$ give $3u^2 \cdot 2 = 6(2x + 1)^2$.
cards.searchQuery: chain rule Leibniz notation dy/du du/dx

cards.title: $h(x) = f(g(x))$ with $g(2) = 3$, $g'(2) = 4$ and $f'(3) = 5$. What is $h'(2)$?
cards.body:
$20$

$h'(2) = f'(g(2)) \cdot g'(2) = f'(3) \cdot 4 = 5 \cdot 4$.

Watch out: evaluate $f'$ at the **inner value** $g(2) = 3$, not at $2$.
cards.searchQuery: chain rule numeric composite derivative f(g(2))

cards.title: $f(1) = 2$, $f'(1) = 3$, $g(1) = 4$, $g'(1) = -1$. What is $(fg)'(1)$?
cards.body:
$10$

$(fg)'(1) = f'(1)g(1) + f(1)g'(1) = 3 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot (-1) = 12 - 2$.

Watch out: the product of the derivatives, $3 \cdot (-1) = -3$, is the classic wrong answer.
cards.searchQuery: product rule numeric example (fg) at 1

cards.title: With $f(1) = 2$, $f'(1) = 3$, $g(1) = 4$, $g'(1) = -1$, what is $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)'(1)$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{7}{8}$

$\frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2} = \frac{3 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot (-1)}{4^2} = \frac{14}{16}$.

Watch out: the minus in the numerator combines with $g'(1) = -1$ to give $+2$.
cards.searchQuery: quotient rule numeric example (f/g) at 1

cards.title: What is the slope of $y = \sin x$ at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{2}$

The slope is $\frac{d}{dx}[\sin x]$ at $\frac{\pi}{3}$, which is $\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$.

Tip: differentiate first, then evaluate; plugging in before differentiating gives the function value $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, not the slope.
cards.searchQuery: slope of sin x at pi/3 derivative cos value

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[x \sin x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\sin x + x\cos x$

Product rule: $(1)(\sin x) + x(\cos x)$.

Watch out: both factors vary, so $\frac{d}{dx}[x\sin x]$ is not $\sin x$ alone, which would only follow if $x$ were a constant.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of x sin x product rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{x\cos x - \sin x}{x^2}$

Quotient rule with $f = \sin x$ and $g = x$: $\frac{\cos x \cdot x - \sin x \cdot 1}{x^2}$.

Watch out: it is not $\frac{\cos x}{1}$; you can't differentiate top and bottom separately.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of sin x over x quotient rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d^{100}}{dx^{100}}[\sin x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\sin x$

The derivatives cycle with period four: $\sin x \to \cos x \to -\sin x \to -\cos x \to \sin x$. Since $100 = 4 \cdot 25$, we are back at the start.

Tip: divide the order by $4$ and use the **remainder** to read off the answer.
cards.searchQuery: 100th derivative of sin x cycle of four

cards.title: $\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}\left[x^n\right] = \,?$ ($n$ a positive integer)
cards.body:
$n!$

Each differentiation brings down the current exponent: $n \cdot (n - 1) \cdots 2 \cdot 1$, leaving the constant $n!$.

Key idea: differentiate once more and you get $0$, so the $(n+1)$st derivative of $x^n$ is $0$.
cards.searchQuery: nth derivative of x^n equals n factorial

cards.title: $\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}\left[e^{2x}\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$2^n e^{2x}$

Each derivative multiplies by the factor $2$ from the chain rule, and $e^{2x}$ stays unchanged.

Example: $\frac{d^3}{dx^3}[e^{2x}] = 8e^{2x}$.
cards.searchQuery: nth derivative of e^(2x) equals 2^n e^(2x)

cards.title: $\dfrac{d^5}{dx^5}\left[x^4 + 3x\right] = \,?$
cards.body:
$0$

Each derivative lowers a polynomial's degree by one, so the fourth derivative is the constant $24$ and the **fifth is zero**.

Key idea: a polynomial of degree $n$ has $(n+1)$st derivative $0$.
cards.searchQuery: fifth derivative of degree four polynomial is zero

cards.title: What does the second derivative $f''(x)$ measure?
cards.body:
The rate of change of the slope $f'$: it tells how the graph **bends** (concavity).

If $f'' > 0$ the slopes increase and the graph is concave up; if $f'' < 0$ it is concave down. In motion, $s''(t)$ is acceleration.

Key idea: $f''$ is the derivative of the derivative, nothing more.
cards.searchQuery: meaning of second derivative rate of change of slope concavity

cards.title: $f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2$. Find $f''(x)$.
cards.body:
$12x^2 - 6$

First derivative: $f'(x) = 4x^3 - 6x$. Differentiate again: $f''(x) = 12x^2 - 6$.

Watch out: differentiate twice, in order; don't jump from $x^4$ to $12x^2$ without keeping the $-6$ from the $-3x^2$ term.
cards.searchQuery: second derivative of x^4 - 3x^2

cards.title: Let $f(x) = x^2(x + 1)^3$. Use logarithmic differentiation to find $f'(1)$.
cards.body:
$28$

$\ln f = 2\ln x + 3\ln(x + 1)$, so $\frac{f'}{f} = \frac{2}{x} + \frac{3}{x + 1}$. At $x = 1$: $f(1) = 8$ and $\frac{f'}{f} = 2 + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{7}{2}$, so $f'(1) = 8 \cdot \frac{7}{2}$.

Tip: the product rule gives the same value: $2 \cdot 8 + 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 28$.
cards.searchQuery: logarithmic differentiation f(x)=x^2(x+1)^3 find f prime 1

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x^{\sin x}\right] = \,?$ ($x > 0$)
cards.body:
$x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x \ln x + \dfrac{\sin x}{x}\right)$

Take logs: $\ln y = \sin x \ln x$. Differentiate with the product rule: $\frac{y'}{y} = \cos x \ln x + \frac{\sin x}{x}$. Then multiply by $y$.

Watch out: the last step is to multiply by $y = x^{\sin x}$, not to leave $\frac{y'}{y}$.
cards.searchQuery: logarithmic differentiation x^(sin x) derivative

cards.title: When is logarithmic differentiation the right tool?
cards.body:
When the **variable is in both the base and the exponent**, or for a messy product, quotient or power of many factors.

Taking $\ln$ turns powers into products and products into sums, which are easier to differentiate.

Example: $\frac{d}{dx}[x^x]$ needs it, while $\frac{d}{dx}[x^3]$ and $\frac{d}{dx}[3^x]$ don't.
cards.searchQuery: when to use logarithmic differentiation variable in base and exponent

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\arccos x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$

It holds for $-1 < x < 1$. Why: $\arccos x = \frac{\pi}{2} - \arcsin x$, so its derivative is the negative of the arcsin derivative.

Tip: each co-function inverse has the opposite sign of its partner.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of arccos x negative 1/sqrt(1-x^2)

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\operatorname{arccot} x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$

It is the negative of $\frac{d}{dx}[\arctan x] = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$, because $\operatorname{arccot} x = \frac{\pi}{2} - \arctan x$ (on its usual range).

Tip: the inverse co-functions never need separate memorization, only a minus sign.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of arccot x negative 1/(1+x^2)

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\arctan 2x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{2}{1 + 4x^2}$

Outside: $\frac{1}{1 + u^2}$ with $u = 2x$, so $\frac{1}{1 + 4x^2}$. Inside: $u' = 2$.

Watch out: $(2x)^2 = 4x^2$, not $2x^2$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of arctan 2x chain rule

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\arcsin\dfrac{x}{2}\right] = \,?$ ($|x| < 2$)
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4 - x^2}}$

Chain rule: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2/4}} \cdot \frac{1}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{1 - x^2/4} = \frac{\sqrt{4 - x^2}}{2}$, the $2$'s cancel.

Tip: this form is the one to recognize in integrals: $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{4 - x^2}} = \arcsin\frac{x}{2} + C$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of arcsin(x/2) chain rule 1/sqrt(4-x^2)

cards.title: Which inverse trig derivatives carry a minus sign?
cards.body:
$\arccos$, $\operatorname{arccot}$ and $\operatorname{arccsc}$: the **co-function** inverses.

Each is the negative of its partner: $\arccos$ vs. $\arcsin$, $\operatorname{arccot}$ vs. $\arctan$, $\operatorname{arccsc}$ vs. $\operatorname{arcsec}$.

Mnemonic: 'co' means a minus sign, just as for $\cos$, $\cot$ and $\csc$.
cards.searchQuery: which inverse trig derivatives have minus signs arccos arccot arccsc

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\sinh x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\cosh x$

With $\sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}$: differentiating gives $\frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2} = \cosh x$.

Tip: $\sinh$ and $\cosh$ behave like $\sin$ and $\cos$ with the minus signs removed.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of hyperbolic sine sinh x equals cosh x

cards.title: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\cosh x] = \,?$
cards.body:
$\sinh x$

With $\cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}$: differentiating gives $\frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2} = \sinh x$.

Watch out: there is **no minus sign**, unlike $\frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] = -\sin x$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of hyperbolic cosine cosh x equals sinh x

cards.title: $xy = 1$. Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ by implicit differentiation.
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{y}{x}$

The left side needs the product rule: $y + x\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{y}{x}$.

Check: solving first gives $y = \frac{1}{x}$, with derivative $-\frac{1}{x^2}$, which equals $-\frac{y}{x}$.
cards.searchQuery: implicit differentiation xy=1 dy/dx equals -y/x

cards.title: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $(3, 3)$ on the curve $x^3 + y^3 = 6xy$.
cards.body:
$-1$

Differentiate: $3x^2 + 3y^2y' = 6y + 6xy'$. Solve: $y' = \frac{2y - x^2}{y^2 - 2x}$. At $(3, 3)$ this is $\frac{6 - 9}{9 - 6} = -1$.

Watch out: $6xy$ needs the product rule, so it contributes both $6y$ and $6xy'$.
cards.searchQuery: implicit differentiation folium x^3+y^3=6xy slope at (3,3)

cards.title: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $(1, -2)$ on the curve $x^2 + xy + y^2 = 3$.
cards.body:
$0$

Differentiate: $2x + y + xy' + 2yy' = 0$, so $y' = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$. At $(1, -2)$ the numerator is $2 - 2 = 0$ and the denominator is $-3$.

So the tangent is **horizontal** there, since the slope is $0$.
cards.searchQuery: implicit differentiation x^2+xy+y^2=3 slope at (1,-2)

cards.title: For $x^2 + y^2 = 25$, find $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ in terms of $y$.
cards.body:
$-\dfrac{25}{y^3}$

From $y' = -\frac{x}{y}$, the quotient rule gives $y'' = -\frac{y - x\,y'}{y^2} = -\frac{y + x^2/y}{y^2} = -\frac{x^2 + y^2}{y^3}$, and $x^2 + y^2 = 25$.

Tip: substitute $y'$ back in, then simplify with the original equation.
cards.searchQuery: second derivative implicit differentiation circle -25/y^3

cards.title: Equation of the tangent line to $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ at $(3, 4)$?
cards.body:
$y = -\dfrac{3}{4}x + \dfrac{25}{4}$

The slope is $-\frac{x}{y} = -\frac{3}{4}$, so $y - 4 = -\frac{3}{4}(x - 3)$, which simplifies to $y = -\frac{3}{4}x + \frac{25}{4}$.

Check: the tangent at a point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius, whose slope there is $\frac{4}{3}$.
cards.searchQuery: tangent line to circle x^2+y^2=25 at (3,4)

cards.title: What are the steps of implicit differentiation?
cards.body:
1. Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$.
2. Whenever you differentiate a $y$-term, attach $\frac{dy}{dx}$ (chain rule).
3. Collect all $\frac{dy}{dx}$ terms on one side.
4. Factor out $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and solve for it.

The answer usually involves both $x$ and $y$, so evaluate it at a point on the curve.

Watch out: $\frac{d}{dx}[y^2] = 2y\frac{dy}{dx}$, and products like $xy$ need the product rule.
cards.searchQuery: steps of implicit differentiation

cards.title: $f(x) = x^5 + x + 1$ and $f(1) = 3$. Find $(f^{-1})'(3)$.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{6}$

$(f^{-1})'(3) = \frac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(3))} = \frac{1}{f'(1)}$, and $f'(x) = 5x^4 + 1$ gives $f'(1) = 6$.

Tip: you never need a formula for $f^{-1}$, only the value $f^{-1}(3) = 1$ read off from $f(1) = 3$.
cards.searchQuery: derivative of inverse function f(x)=x^5+x+1 at 3

cards.title: Differentiate $e^y = x$ implicitly to find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ for $y = \ln x$, in terms of $x$.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{x}$

Differentiating gives $e^y \frac{dy}{dx} = 1$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{e^y}$. Since $e^y = x$, this is $\frac{1}{x}$.

Key idea: the same trick (differentiate $f(y) = x$) produces every inverse-function derivative.
cards.searchQuery: derive derivative of ln x implicit differentiation e^y = x

cards.title: Equation of the tangent line to $y = e^x$ at $x = 0$?
cards.body:
$y = x + 1$

Point: $(0, 1)$. Slope: $\frac{d}{dx}[e^x] = e^x$, which is $1$ at $x = 0$.

Key idea: this line is the linear approximation $e^x \approx 1 + x$ for small $x$.
cards.searchQuery: tangent line to e^x at x=0 y=x+1

cards.title: Equation of the tangent line to $y = \ln x$ at $x = 1$?
cards.body:
$y = x - 1$

Point: $(1, 0)$. Slope: $\frac{d}{dx}[\ln x] = \frac{1}{x}$, which is $1$ at $x = 1$.

Watch out: the point is $(1, 0)$, not $(1, 1)$, since $\ln 1 = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: tangent line to ln x at x=1 y=x-1

cards.title: Equation of the normal line to $y = x^2$ at $x = 1$?
cards.body:
$y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + \dfrac{3}{2}$

The tangent slope is $2x = 2$, so the normal slope is $-\frac{1}{2}$. Through $(1, 1)$: $y - 1 = -\frac{1}{2}(x - 1)$.

Watch out: flip the tangent slope **and** change its sign.
cards.searchQuery: normal line to y=x^2 at x=1 equation

cards.title: At which values of $x$ does $y = x^3 - 3x$ have a horizontal tangent?
cards.body:
$x = 1$ and $x = -1$.

A horizontal tangent means $y' = 0$: $3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1) = 0$.

The points are $(1, -2)$ and $(-1, 2)$. Don't give only the $x$-values when a question asks for the **points**.
cards.searchQuery: where does y=x^3-3x have horizontal tangent

cards.title: $s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$ for $t \ge 0$. At what times is the particle at rest?
cards.body:
$t = 1$ and $t = 3$.

At rest means $v(t) = s'(t) = 0$: $3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t - 1)(t - 3)$.

Watch out: being at rest at an instant is not the same as being at the origin; the position there is $s(1) = 4$ and $s(3) = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: particle at rest velocity zero position function t^3-6t^2+9t
